subtype: Stage 4: Parent takes sides by accident [Observer]
passage: In the clinic waiting room, Elizabeth, the nurse, was filling a form when she heard a crash. Six-year-old Anjali and her little brother Mihir had pulled at the same picture book. Mihir fell and started howling. Their father jumped up, scooped Mihir into his arms and turned to Anjali. "You're older! Be sensible!" Anjali's arms dropped. "But he..." "No buts." Anjali sat back on her chair alone, swinging her legs hard. Elizabeth saw her wipe her eyes with her sleeve and stare at the floor.

qa.q: What were Anjali and Mihir pulling at?
qa.a: They were pulling at the same picture book.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when her father said, "No buts"?
qa.a: She felt blamed and unheard, and sad that her father took Mihir's side without listening.

qa.q: What could the father have done instead?
qa.a: He could comfort Mihir and also ask Anjali what happened, so she doesn't feel that being older means she always gets blamed.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see Anjali after the scolding?
qa.a: Elizabeth notices a hurt little girl sitting alone, wiping her eyes and staring at the floor.

grounding: It shows a parent rushing to the crying younger child and scolding the older one with you are older, be sensible, leaving her feeling blamed.

subtype: Stage 4: Parent takes sides by accident [Observer]
passage: I'm Maria, and I live next door to Simran's family. Yesterday I heard a scream. Simran, who is five, and her baby brother were both holding the same ball. The baby started crying. Their mother came running. She picked up the baby and said, "Simran, you're the big sister! Why can't you just give it?" Simran said, "But it's mine!" Her mother said, "You're older, be sensible." Simran went quiet and sat in the corner of the balcony. I don't know what she was thinking. But this is the third time this week I've heard the same words.

qa.q: What were Simran and her baby brother both holding?
qa.a: They were both holding the same ball.

qa.q: What might Simran be feeling in the corner of the balcony?
qa.a: She might feel blamed and sad, maybe thinking her mother loves the baby more because she is older.

qa.q: How could Simran's mother handle it differently?
qa.a: She could comfort the baby and also listen to Simran's side, so being older doesn't always mean being the one scolded.

qa.q: What does Maria notice about the pattern?
qa.a: Maria notices that the same words, "You're older, be sensible," have been said three times this week, which worries Maria. 😔

grounding: It illustrates a parent comforting the crying younger child and scolding the older one with you're older, be sensible, a repeated pattern.

subtype: Stage 4: Parent takes sides by accident [Observer]
passage:
Monday. Ammachi was shelling peas on the veranda when little Tessa's juice spilled. Mummy rushed in, picked Tessa up and told Jomon, "You're older! Be sensible!" Jomon hadn't touched it.

Wednesday. Tessa pulled Jomon's hair. Jomon pushed her away. Tessa wailed. Mummy came running. "Jomon! She's small!" Ammachi saw Jomon's face crumple.

Friday. Jomon kicked Tessa's doll across the room for no reason. Tessa cried. Mummy scolded him again.

Later, Ammachi found Jomon under the table. "Mummy loves Tessa more," he whispered. "Because I'm big."

Ammachi pulled him onto her lap. She knew she needed to talk to her daughter-in-law that evening.

qa.q: What was Ammachi doing when she heard the crash on Monday?
qa.a: Shelling peas on the veranda.

qa.q: What was Ammachi feeling when she saw Jomon's face crumple?
qa.a: She felt sad and concerned, seeing that he felt blamed again for something he hadn't done.

qa.q: What could Mummy do differently when Tessa cries?
qa.a: Calm both children and listen to each before blaming Jomon, instead of repeating "you're older, be sensible".

qa.q: What has Jomon come to believe about being older?
qa.a: He believes being older means Mummy loves him less, which feeds his angry behaviour.

grounding: Over a week Ammachi watches Mummy rush to the crying younger child and scold Jomon, teaching him that being older means less love and fuelling the next round.

subtype: Stage 4: Parent takes sides by accident [Observer]
passage:
It had rained for three days, and the children hadn't been outside once. Seema Bua sat knitting in the corner of the small flat.

Jassi snatched Gurpreet's toy truck. Gurpreet grabbed it back. Jassi howled.

Their mother rushed in and scooped Jassi up. "Gurpreet! You're the big brother. Be sensible!"

"She took it first!"

Gurpreet pressed his forehead to the window. Seema Bua saw his shoulders shake. It was the third time that day.

That night Seema Bua quietly told her sister-in-law, "He thinks being older means being loved less."

qa.q: How long had it rained?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What was Seema Bua feeling as she watched Gurpreet at the window?
qa.a: She felt concerned and sad, seeing him blamed again and his shoulders shaking.

qa.q: What could the mother try instead of "You're older, be sensible"?
qa.a: Separate the children, listen to both sides, and see that Jassi took the truck first, so Gurpreet doesn't feel blamed every time.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet experience being told to be sensible?
qa.a: He feels unfairly blamed and less loved, since he was only taking back his own truck.

grounding: On a rainy day Seema Bua sees the mother rush to the crying younger child and scold older Gurpreet repeatedly, teaching him being older means less love.

subtype: Stage 4: Parent takes sides by accident [Observer]
passage:
Harsha aunty from next door had brought laddoos and was on the sofa when it happened.

Little Inaya was climbing onto Yusuf's back. Yusuf said, "Stop!" and shook her off. Inaya fell onto the rug, crying.

Their mother ran in, picked up Inaya and turned to Yusuf. "You're the elder one! Be sensible!"

Yusuf's lip trembled. "She was climbing on me."

"She's small. You're big."

Harsha aunty watched Yusuf walk slowly to his room. He didn't slam the door. That was worse.

Later, as she was leaving, she said gently, "He was just trying to get her off, you know." The mother looked surprised, then thoughtful.

qa.q: What did Harsha aunty bring?
qa.a: A box of laddoos.

qa.q: What was Harsha aunty feeling as Yusuf walked slowly to his room?
qa.a: She felt sad and uneasy, noticing that his quiet reaction was somehow worse than a slammed door.

qa.q: What small step did Harsha aunty take that could help?
qa.a: She gently pointed out to the mother that Yusuf was only trying to get Inaya off, which may help her listen before blaming next time.

qa.q: How does Yusuf feel after being scolded?
qa.a: He feels hurt and unfairly blamed, as if being older means being loved less.

grounding: Harsha aunty, a neighbour, sees a mother rush to the crying toddler and scold older Yusuf, and gently points out the pattern.

subtype: Stage 4: Parent takes sides by accident [Observer]
passage:
"Ammi! Afreen pushed me!" Zayan wailed from the balcony.
Their Ammi, Rukhsana, rushed out and scooped him up. "Afreen! You're older, you should be sensible. How many times?"
"But he tore my drawing first..."
"Enough. Say sorry to your brother."
Afreen's chin shook. "Sorry," she mumbled, and ran to her room.
Sunaina Aunty, visiting from next door with ladoos, had seen it all. Softly she said, "Rukhsana, the drawing really was torn. I saw."
Rukhsana paused, Zayan on her hip. "Oh. I only heard him crying."
From the bedroom came Afreen's voice, small and loud at once: "You always take his side!"

qa.q: What had Zayan done to Afreen's drawing?
qa.a: He tore Afreen's drawing first.

qa.q: What does Sunaina Aunty's soft comment suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seemed concerned and a little uncomfortable, sensing that Afreen had been blamed unfairly.

qa.q: How could Rukhsana handle the next fight differently?
qa.a: She could pause, calm both children and ask each what happened before scolding, instead of siding with whoever is crying.

qa.q: What is it like for Afreen to hear 'You're older, you should be sensible' again?
qa.a: Afreen feels blamed and hurt, as if being older means being loved less, and bursts out that Ammi always takes his side.

grounding: Shows a parent rushing to the crying younger child and scolding the older one, who feels blamed again, as noticed by a visiting neighbour.
